utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we start on the question of evidence today, I have two matters I wish to raise in relation to expert reports. Mr. Hannis, you expressed concern before about the timing of the disclosure of the report by Radinovic. It is now available. He's scheduled, I think, to give evidence next week. That means that the normal provisions of Rule 94 would have to be modified to enable that to happen. Do you ever a clear position on that or is it something you're still reflecting on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I am still reflecting on it. I can tell you if he is permitted to testify as an expert we do wish to cross-examine him. I can commit to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would indicate that we would propose to file some objections to portions of his reported based on my initial viewing of it that I think may not be relevant, and we also have an argument to make to him similar to our argument that we made regarding Professor Markovic at the beginning of the case that we think he's too close to the Defence side of the case and he's too biased to testify as an expert. I know we failed on our application regarding Professor Markovic, but I think there's grounds to make that argument again and I would propose to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it still possible though to have all this done and give evidence next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find that very difficult. I just got the report today in English. I just got the updated report today in English which is some 30 pages longer than what we got a couple of days ago. In addition I'm trying to prepare for the possible cross-examination of General Ojdanic if he indeed does testify and during both those things at the same time is extremely burdensome. I don't know if the Court is willing to consider the possibility of having the Defence expert testify later, at some other stage in the case. I know you would like to conclude this accused's portion of the case now or as soon as possible, but I propose that as an alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic, it is obvious that there are potential difficulties for the Prosecution in meeting a time scale that would enable Radinovic to give evidence next week, so some other option may have to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I find it hard to take a position now in view of what Mr. Hannis has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One possibility would be to have him testify at the end of the case like other experts which we were told would be the course followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I leave that to the Trial Chamber to decide, but I believe that the other Defence teams should have their say as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's leave this until tomorrow and have a brief discussion then once everyone has had a chance to think further of it. It will be clearer in our minds. The second issue is also one of expert evidence and that's the report of Branislav Simonovic. Mr. Ivetic, I have been advised of the various discussions you've been having with -- just give me a moment, please. Various discussions you've been having with the CLSS on this subject. They are not likely, as I see it, to bear fruit. On the other hand, the issues that you are discussing are matters which you can clearly make submissions to the Trial Chamber about. The issue has arisen before, and it's one that seems a matter for us to resolve in due course in the light of all the evidence. The witness himself can give evidence about it, and it seems to me that the application you've made is not really going to take the matter any further or advance it at this stage. Now, do you see a particular reason why we should address the issue at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it comes with the culmination of the growing set of headaches we've had recently with translations where we find that what is being translated is not what witnesses are saying and in essence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's concentrate on this one this is a very specific example in which the position of CLSS is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have proposed that we use the acronym PJP and that's what we'd still like to do to avoid any confusion and for our part we're going to try and use the full Serbian name of the unit when dealing with the expert when he is here to testify. So from our side we are going to try to alleviate any confusion over -- over that -- that issue so that the evidence can be led and that the expert can be satisfied that his expert opinion is being expressed with the words that he -- that he chooses to use to explain the various organs and functioning of the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But bearing in mind that you have every opportunity to make whatever submissions you wish, you -- do you intend to insist on this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have so much work that having to make submission on an issue like this could add a hardship. I don't know exactly what kind of submissions are necessary. If the Court is aware of the issue and keeps that in mind when listening to the testimony, I think that serves the purpose of -- of us bringing it to the Court's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think it would assist greatly if this application were withdrawn. It would make no -- it's going to make no difference to how the matter's dealt with in the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll check with the counsel and we'll have an answer for you later today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tomorrow when we deal with the other issue as well because they're both related to the determination of the date by which any submissions by the Prosecution ought to be made in relation to these two reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear further on both these matters tomorrow. Now, Mr. Visnjic, can we start with the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before we move on to the evidence, I would briefly like to address the Trial Chamber. It has to do with the witness who is supposed to testify now. I think we should move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the videolink now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Farkas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell us what position you had in the military hierarchy in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: In 1999, I was chief of the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note while the witness is speaking could all other microphones please be switched off. We cannot hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When were you appointed to that position?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I was appointed to that position on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did that happen? How did you get appointed to that position as chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Before that position, I was assistant minister of defence for Civil Defence and through the cabinet of the federal minister I was invited 10 or 15 days before the aggression started to President Milosevic's office. President Milosevic presented his views and this possibility of appointing me to this particular position.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At that time did you talk about the position that General Dimitrijevic would have who is your predecessor as chief of the security administration?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I asked him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what were you told then?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The president said to me then that Mr. Aco Dimitrijevic would be appointed Assistant Federal Minister of Defence to unify the work of the security services at the level of all of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Civilian and military security that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, when you came to head the security administration did you carry out any major personnel changes?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I did not carry out any major personnel changes. Only the necessary ones envisaged by our regulations in relation to wartime establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General Gajic testified before this Tribunal, and he spoke at length about the work of the security administration and what it did. I don't want to go through all of that with you now. I want to ask you about the following, though: General Gajic testified before this Court that at the very outset of the war there was a change in the system of information flow and the system of communications from lower to higher security organs.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why these changes took place?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is only natural that once a war starts a new system of communications is established. There is wartime formation of all units, staffs, and commands. The communications used until then had probably been intercepted and the codes must have been broken. So that is one reason, technical. The second is the speed of information flows through secure lines that existed between the subordinate units, those two -- or, rather, between the units that were subordinated and the Supreme Command Staff. The security organs are integrated in these staffs and these commands, and then along the chain of command they informed their superior commands up the chain up to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what would be the basic document, then, through which reporting was supposed to go during the war in the field of security?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The basic document was the regular and extraordinary combat report from subordinate units to the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand from what General Gajic said, up until the beginning of the war there was direct communication, line of communication. By that I mean frequent or regular communication between the security organs along the security line, but when the war began in accordance with what you said this line of communication went through the commands of the subordinate units and through combat reports. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. You understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, why did you in early May go to Kosovo? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the first reason was that we had a situation there. Some information was not specific enough, especially as regards to security affairs. And then the Chief of the General Staff -- or, rather, of the Supreme Command Staff ordered me to go down to Kosovo and to see where the problem lay, because he suspected that those reports were not reaching him regularly, and he thought that what he was getting was not sufficient for his decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, once you went down to Kosovo, and let me repeat that was in early May, what did you find there? How long did you spend there, and what information did you gather there?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I spent a short time there, just two days, and I reported to the commander of the army as per usual procedure. He had known that I would come. And I did learn something about the way that the security organs in the lower organisation and units were functioning. I learned that they were carrying out their tasks properly, in a very good manner, and my knowledge from the level of the brigade and onwards at the regular reporting with their commands and their commanders, this was all made part of those reports and all this information finally reached the Supreme Command Staff of the chain of command through those reports. But I did encounter some problems that were presented there. I did learn that there were some problems in terms of vertical cooperation between the military organs and security organs and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the reports that you got at the General Staff up until that time and what you learned in this previous period of time, were there any differences in what you had been getting up until that time, up the line that you received those combat reports and what you were able to establish in the field.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, there were differences, and the difference was that some crimes were committed and some of the measures that had been prescribed had not been complied with. Reports in those units up the level of the brigade were regularly reported to their superior commands, but this information never reached us. So I learned that criminal offences were being committed, crimes, including crimes, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came back to Belgrade, sir, what -- what did you do in relation to this issue?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I first met with my collegium, and I informed my collegium about the results and what I had learned down there at Kosovo. After that, immediately after that, I reported orally to the chief of the General Staff about what I had noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: His reaction was a strong one because of these events, and at that time I was unable to give him quite some specific details because I had been there for a very short time, and he wanted all that to be established once again. He wanted all the details, and then he said that he would report to the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And do you know or can you recall whether General Ojdanic had in fact informed the Supreme Commander, President Milosevic, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. He informed Mr. Milosevic immediately about this problem. They discussed it. Milosevic ordered something, and I know, because he told me that, the chief of staff of the Supreme Command told me that Milosevic would convene a meeting on the 17th of May on the topic of the way in which those problems that I noted down in Kosovo could be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But before this meeting on the 17th of May, you did have a meeting within the army of Yugoslavia on this very same topic. Could you tell us something more about that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, before this meeting, the chief of staff of the Supreme Command decided to call the commander of the 3rd Army, Mr. Pavkovic, in order to prepare for this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could you please describe to us briefly what happened at that meeting on the 16th, if I'm not mistaken. That's based on what General Gajic had told us in his evidence, but I may have gone too far with this question. According to General Gajic's evidence, this meeting was held on the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the chief of staff of the Supreme Command asked the 3rd Army commander to report to him on the overall security situation in -- in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army, area of the focus of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what did General Pavkovic report to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: As far as I know, because I had not had any contacts, major contacts, with him before that, he told us -- he told you all of us that there were some problems and that crimes had been committed in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Army and that some army of Yugoslavia troops participated in the commission of those crimes. So he gave an overall assessment of the security situation in Kosovo, and he added this information too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you remember who attended this meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: In addition to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and the 3rd Army commander; I was there, General Vasiljevic my deputy was there; and so was general -- or at that time I think he was still a colonel, Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the information that you received from General Pavkovic at that time was something that was relatively new for you. You didn't know any of that with the exception of what you learned during your brief stay in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We were not aware of the details that he presented to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us or describe briefly the meeting at the -- at President Milosevic's on the 17th of May, 1999. Who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, at that meeting, apart from President Milosevic, there was General Ojdanic; Rade Markovic who was the head of the state security there representing the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior; I was there; my deputy Aco Vasiljevic; and General Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly how the meeting progressed?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The previous day at the meeting with General Pavkovic we agreed on an order in which we would present the problems at this forthcoming meeting, and we agreed that General Pavkovic would make some opening remarks and that he would report to the president about the military, political, and security situation in Kosovo. He was the first one to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And General Pavkovic, as far as I understood from General Gajic's evidence, he repeated what he had already told you the day before at the meeting on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He repeated all that, and he stressed that at that forum. He stressed this problem. I think that Sainovic was also there at that meeting. I forgot to mention that. Yes, Mr. Sainovic was present at that meeting. General Pavkovic at that meeting put a great emphasis on the problems with the cooperation with the MUP, and he even proposed that a commission be set up, a joint commission, that would deal with all those problems and control all those security problems, problems regarding the crimes, a commission that would control both the army and the MUP. And Mr. Sainovic agreed with this proposal made by General Pavkovic, and he said that that should be a state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, was there any discussion about the resubordination of MUP at that meeting or just the cooperation with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the problem of the resubordination actually led to the problems that occurred down there, because in the military chain of command the order of -- for the resubordination was disseminated to all the military units, and this was not done in the MUP for the resubordination of the MUP organisational units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What were the conclusions reached at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, many topics were presented there. The crimes were discussed, the crimes that were detected, prosecuted, that were still in some kind of procedure. The president ordered, because the minister of the interior was not present at that meeting, the president ordered that Rade Markovic should meet with the minister as urgently as possible and to resolve those problems including the problem of the para-police forces that were present there on the ground. I had learned about that and General Pavkovic presented that problem at the meeting. And the president ordered that Rade Markovic as soon as possible, that the para-police forces should be removed from Kosovo as soon as possible, that the perpetrators, known perpetrators of crimes from those formations should be investigated, should be brought before a Court and those units should not come to that area again. That was one of the conclusions that the president presented to the MUP. As for us, he told us that because of the fierceness of the airstrikes and the current situation, according to the assessment made by General Pavkovic, he said that the army should take everything it could to prevent even a single square foot of our territory from falling into the enemy hands. He ordered that the defence efforts along the borders with Albania and Macedonia should be increased. And because there were some para-police and paramilitary formations in the territory of Yugoslavia, he ordered that if necessary that the Drim [as interpreted] should be closed off to prevent the incursion of any forces that could commit those crimes that could later be ascribed to the police and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, at 5 -- 15, line 18, you said Drim?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, I said Drina, the Drina River. The border along the Drina River facing Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened after that order -- that meeting? What orders did General Ojdanic issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment before you embark on that question. Could I be clear about one thing, Mr. Farkas. You've told us about the meeting of quite a number of people with President Milosevic, including representatives of the military and the Ministry of the Interior. When that meeting came to an end was there a smaller meeting, a smaller group, who stayed behind and discussed matters further with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. General Ojdanic took us there immediately, and all the representatives of the military accompanied him. And as we -- I don't know how people left the room, in what order. I merely know that we all headed out with General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "all," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to the representatives of the army, myself, General Vasiljevic, and General Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in answering, you've omitted any reference to General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Pavkovic. I apologise. So all the soldiers, all the military officers accompanied General Ojdanic out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've heard some evidence, I think, that General Pavkovic stayed. Are you clear that he left with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that I'm certain that all of us just stood up and went out, this group of officer around General Ojdanic. It seems to me that all of us generals of the army headed out in a single group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be I'm mistaken in my recollection of that matter, and I shall check it. Please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what orders were given you immediately after that meeting by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: As we were still walking going out of the meeting, while we were still in that group he was issuing orders to build up measures of security facing the border. And to me specifically he said that I should form an extremely strong group of security organs and come with him, inspect the basic units and inspect security organs in the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you indeed set up that team?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I immediately set up that team headed by General Vasiljevic. There was also General Lajic on that team.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Gajic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: From the testimony of General Gajic and General Vasiljevic, we know that they did go to Kosovo. In the course of their stay there, did you have any communication with them?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, we did communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on to that in a moment, but I want to ask you, do you know that General Ojdanic perhaps gave orders to other administrations, other organs of the General Staff in connection with that meeting in President Milosevic's office?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that later, but I can't say exactly when. Maybe that afternoon. There was talk within that group that he should urgently issue orders asking reports from the judiciary on the crimes that had been committed and the measures taken in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you said a moment ago that you did communicate with General Vasiljevic and General Gajic while they were in Kosovo. May the Defence Exhibit 3D633 be prepared, please.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's a report from the 2nd of June, 1999, at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you told us that this report took place on the 2nd of June, 1999. Were you present?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On page 1, both in English and in Serbian, we see that below your name there are certain notes.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will be asking you about the part of those notes that begin with the words -- that's line 6 below your name that begins with the words: "Taking measures in connection with the events in Cetinje." Sorry -- correction: "Taking measures to redress the situation in the Pristina Corps."

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what's written.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Then two lines below we see: "In Kosovo misdeeds are being -- crimes are being committed by our units in Kosovo. Reports on these acts are not going through regular channels or lines of command." The next sentence: "Are serious things happening that the global public is aware of?" There must be a problem on this record here. Did you have any information, any specific information when you made this report?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: At that time, that was towards the end of the war operations, we had certain problems with some units. One part of the 7th Brigade had left their positions even before. There were disruptions. People were losing their nerve have especially among the reservists and there were security problems. That was on the one hand. On the other hand, there was some members of the reserve force that took advantage of the overall situation to commit criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And when you say that the reports about this were not going through regular channels or lines of command, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I meant the regular reports that should have gone up the line of command through brigades, corps, armies to the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you told me that you had certain indications even before you came to Kosovo, before you first went to visit Kosovo in end April, early May, what kind of indications did you have that were not in line with the combat reports?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: It was the time of the most intensive operations, and a large number of reservists were in Kosovo, up to 15.000 men, and the scale of these operations and events posed a problem in itself. These problems were not regularly reported on through the regular channels and up the line of command to the Supreme Command Staff. But apart from these security organs that were parts of units, that were part of the units that were directly subordinated to the commanders that formed an integral part of their staffs and that participated in the drafting of reports, apart from those security organs that took care of the intern security of units there were so-called counter-intelligence groups that were protecting units from outside assaults on the security from outside threats. They were directly subordinated, and it was from them that I learned that some crimes were being committed but also that they are being prosecuted. Some are already before courts. But there was none of that in the regular combat reports. Those were the indications I had that prompted the commander of the Supreme Command Staff to tell me to go there myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'd like Exhibit 3D493 to be prepared. General, when did Generals Vasiljevic and Gajic and other members of their team return from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Sometime around the 7th, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us, when they returned did they make their reports, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: They reported verbally to their senior staff meeting outlining their assessment of the operation and work of security organs within basic units, that is brigades, and their assessment was positive saying that within their competencies and to the extent of their abilities they're working well detecting crimes and criminal acts and trying in those difficult wartime conditions to prepare them for prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, 1999, did you report that to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- first of all, do you have the Serbian version typewritten, printed, or in longhand?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I have the printed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I believe in this exhibit there's another attachment which has the printed B/C/S version. General, here on page 1 we see the beginning of your presentation. It has mainly to do with events in Montenegro. Can we have page 2, please, in B/C/S. That is, could you look at page 2 in B/C/S, especially the passage after the line that says: "There are problems, humanitarian crime." And then the second line says: "A complete analysis has been made, led by the deputy chief of the security administration." You are talking here about the report made to you by Generals Vasiljevic and Gajic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us a bit more. What exactly did you say to the Supreme Command Staff?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, based on this evaluation they made, I've already said that the security organs down there, as parts of their respective commands, took part in the work of the commands and reported all their findings. And the inspecting organs that I sent found out that over 90 per cent, 95 per cent of these criminal acts were prosecuted. The perpetrators were under investigation or arrest and that some active-duty personnel were among the perpetrators. That is, both soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you reported that you had issued certain orders to you security organs?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. I included that because by that time it was already a certainty that we would withdraw from Kosovo. It was the 76th day of the war, and of course I issued orders to our organs. I had sent reinforcement and assistance to the basic units, primarily the Pristina Corps, in order to organise the pull-out of all the forces out of Kosovo in keeping with the Kumanova agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, could we now look at page 4 in B/C/S. And it's page 4 in English. At the top of the page there's a sentence that I don't understand. You uttered it. "There are incidents where pellets are thrown in fields and ignited by heat." What does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This is a reference to the NATO aviation. In addition to bombs and other projectiles, that's before our pull-out from the territory but after the decision had been made, we analysed those pellets that they ejected, caused fire and destroyed farms. Those pellets took fire under the sun. It was self-ignition, self-combustion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, what did General Ojdanic order regarding your presentation, that is, the conclusions and findings of your controller team in Kosovo that --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: He gave them credit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: He gave them credit. He commended the security administration and the team that worked in Kosovo trying to document -- document all that was impermissible under international laws of war as he had ordered himself in his prior orders. So he commended the security organs on all levels because under those difficult wartime circumstances they a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, General, that we saw your presentation and we know that there were certain problems. Where would you say was the problem in providing information about crimes that were possibly committed?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the problem was that at certain levels -- the lower levels the job was done well, but at certain levels this information underwent filtering and certain processing before it reached the Supreme Command Staff. The reports were not specific enough, were not clear enough, and they were not comprehensive enough, so they did not enable a good evaluation, a proper evaluation. Because the war was not only in Kosovo. There was war on our entire territory. And some of these phenomena had repercussions and happened in other territories, Montenegro and in other regions. So the people who worked on this did not properly report to the Supreme Command Staff on what they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you to have a look at 3D487, please. General, you have the document before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: These are tasks that the chief of the Supreme Command Staff set at a meeting held on the 8th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention to paragraphs 1 and 3 of this document, and could you give us your comments regarding paragraphs 1 and 3?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: "The military judicial organs shall resolve criminal reports according to the following priorities: First, violations of provisions of international law; second, crime in the Yugoslav army; third, desertion; and four, other crimes, other criminal offences." That is to say that through this paragraph he reacts to everything that was learned and sublimated until then, and he even says in which order organs should take measures and work. And what was the other paragraph you asked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. "Monitor paramilitary organisations in the territory (objective, forces, leadership, locations, and so on) take action falling within your own remit and inform the MUP of the Republic of Serbia about that." A comment in this respect would be that when the decision was made to withdraw the forces the army and the MUP from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija certain problems were created in the area among the army, among the civilian population in terms of carrying this out. The officers were there with their families. They had their marching orders. They were retreating. And the status of their families had not been resolved fully. That moment was taken advantage of by destructive forces that wanted to remain in Kosovo, and also military conscripts on the condition that their weapons were left to them. That situation had to be dealt with and one had to leave the area with one's head high, and all other problems should have been resolved through political and diplomatic channels and means.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, as far as I understood the further course of events this was rather successfully prevented and no military troops remained in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Among the Serbian population that remained in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's right. This task was carried out consistently, in a dignified manner, regardless of these problems that we came across. That is to say the security organs, the army MUP and officers of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. One more question. After the end of the war the security administration continued working on uncovering perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. We continued, because many problems were being dealt with only in its -- in their initial stages. That is to say that it was the pre-investigation stage. However, a great many of these problems we could not resolve because as we withdrew from that territory we had no access to the territory. UNMIK forces came to the area and the paramilitary units of the Kosovo Albanians remained there. They had already organised strong military formations, so we did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Let it be precise for the transcript. When I asked you on page 25, lines 13, 14, 15, whether you continued to work on finding the perpetrators of crimes, I meant crimes -- or, rather, war crimes. I meant violations of international humanitarian law. Are you giving me answers in that spirit?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, yes, precisely in that spirit. These crimes were being dealt with in an initial stage, but we continued within the framework that we had then, because when peace was proclaimed -- or, rather, when there was no more state of war, military courts were disbanded and then civilian courts took over the jurisdiction for resolving these problem, that is to say the gravest crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you please look at 3D1063.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document, this time of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, the security administration, dated the 13th of August, 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what the basic motive was for this document -- or, rather, for this order?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The basic motive was to deal with crimes, particularly war crimes, committed during the course of the war -- or, rather, investigations and the appropriate procedure to continue. And there was a special group of people for that, especially in the 1st Army, whose territory was the best regulated, and security administrations were duty-bound to set up teams and to continue intensively investigations of all war crimes committed during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, just a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving -- before moving to another area, Mr. Visnjic, may I ask the general one question? General, can you give us an example of a violation of international humanitarian law that you discovered and were able to report on in the course of this investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this investigation, well, I could not give specific examples because for the most part this moved to the jurisdiction of civilian courts. That is to say that everything that had started in Kosovo from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Part of the sentence missing, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As military courts were dissolved, then cases were handed over to certain courts in the field, and I have no further reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have misunderstood. During the period from your appointment and the investigation you were carrying out through your staff and on which you ultimately - sorry, just a moment - and on which you ultimately reported to the Chief of the General Staff on the 8th of June, can you give me an example of an alleged violation of international humanitarian law that was unearthed during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are drastic examples. For example, in one unit, I wouldn't know exactly which one it was, a group headed by an officer, as a matter of fact, committed crimes and killed over 10 people, I think, ethnic Albanians, and they threw them into a well, for example. That was the most drastic case that was resolved afterwards, after it was discovered by the security organs and the commands. There were other cases of rape and so on and so forth, but this was a very drastic case, even more so since an officer took part in this, an officer from the army of Yugoslavia. This was dealt with. The prosecution was carried out. It was taken to court. Well, this is a drastic example that I can recall at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I will try to ask you something in relation to Judge Bonomy's question. When we were preparing for your testimony here and in relation to what you said in the Milosevic case, you had a correction in your evidence given in the Milosevic case in relation to information concerning the crime committed in the village of Izbica. Can you tell us what this correction referred to?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This correction refers to the following: I made a permutation of the date of that event. This was reported to me after my team came back from Kosovo. I and all of us were quite surprised that this happened sometime in the beginning of the war and that we were finding out about it only then. However, from the briefing, we realised when this was discovered, when these graves were discovered, that the MUP organs came there for an on-site investigation and of the army of Yugoslavia too. An exhumation was carried out and also a post-mortem. I was convinced during my testimony at Mr. Milosevic's trial in view of the date when this happened and in view of what they reported to me on the 7th, these organs of mine, that of course this had to go through the chain of command and reach the Supreme Command Staff. However, later on I realised that this report concerning that incident did not reach the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Actually, during your testimony in the Milosevic trial you said that you learned about that on the basis of a combat report.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But actually, there is no such report. Am I not right? Is that your testimony now?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's right. The problem is that the mistake is mine. It is my understanding that when military investigation organs go out that the commands are duty-bound, especially when speaking of a volume of that magnitude that it is only natural that this should arrive through command channels, through regular reporting channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Just one more question. Do you know from the moment when you came to the General Staff whether there was some plan on expelling the Albanian population across the border involve -- and that the military and security organs were involved in such a plan?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No. I know of no such plan. The existence of such a plan, no. I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions of this witness, Your Honours. I believe that I have stuck to my original time schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you're even within it. Mr. Visnjic, can you give us a reference to the Milosevic transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you give me a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a suitable time to break and we will resume at 10 minutes to 4.00. We will break at this time, General, and resume your evidence in 20 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is in response to your question about the reference where general wanted to modify his evidence in Milosevic trial. That's at page 46457, lines 13 through 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farkas, you will now be cross-examined by a number of counsel, the first of those will be Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I'm John Ackerman and I represent General Pavkovic and I have a few questions I want to ask you this afternoon. One of the things that has come up in this trial deals with -- there's been a lot of talk about volunteers coming into the military and psychological concerns regarding those people and so forth. The question I want to ask you has, I guess, some relationship to that. I understand that persons were removed from the army due to behavioural or psychological problems. Are you aware of any of those kind of incidents?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. During the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: During the war, when the influx of volunteers grew in number, the Chief of the General Staff -- or, rather, of the Supreme Command Staff issued a very detailed order regulating all the issues or possible problems related to the volunteers. This was a very complex order that encompassed all those elements, everything that a person who is putting on a uniform should do in order to be responsible for his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you not about that but about if someone was removed from the army for behavioural problems or psychological problems, were any steps taken to keep that person from coming back into the forces in some way by maybe a different route, through the police or some other way? Were any steps taken to make sure when that person was removed they stayed removed?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of the Supreme Command Staff issued yet another order that dealt with those issues. Every soldier and in particular every volunteer has his file that accompanies him, a file that where all the data is entered, the reasons for the discharge, and the military territorial organs were obliged under that order to inform about the reasons why this person was recently discharged, to inform the MUP organs in the territory as for the reasons why this volunteer was turned back, so that any problems that might occur could be dealt with, that the weapons be taken away from this person, and that this person be monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of any steps taken before March 24th, before the bombing started, to advise and train personnel of the army regarding the international laws of war?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the bombing started, I was on a different post, but through the Ministry of Defence and through the General Staff courses were organised, courses for officers, and in those courses the officers were told about the international humanitarian law and the laws -- the rules of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know if any steps were taken to -- to provide that information to each of the soldiers that was actually going out in the field?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: When the war started, the administration for morale pursuant to an order of the Chief of the General Staff brochures were put out. They contained appropriate quotes from the conventions on humanitarian law and law of war. I think there were four pages, pocket size. This was enclosed in plastic and every soldier was given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: These were laminated, basically wallet-sized documents that were given to every soldier. Is that -- is that the case?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know if you ever received any information about persons coming across the border from Albania dressed in VJ uniforms, speaking Serbian, who committed several crimes as if they were VJ members.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We received information about those border incidents, about the crossings, and you have to divide those incidents in two parts. The information of this kind about the incidents that occurred in 1998. I know less about those because I was not in the VJ at the time. I was in the defence ministry. But some information did reach us about those incidents. They did reach me. And afterwards, during the war, that was within my remit and those things did happen. So crimes were committed. Buildings were burnt, set on fire, and some crimes were committed in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that -- that information that you received, then, about these people you were able to verify through investigations conducted by security personnel or how?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, some of this information was verified, and certain combat activities were launched against those persons. Those persons were being uncovered, but some remained undetected. They were either pushed back from the territory or they dispersed because of those combat activities aimed at them, and some must have been killed in those clashes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us a specific example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as for the pre-war events in 1998, I have two examples that I remember. A large group of Albanians who were armed, they even had horses, they were ambushed and a large number were killed. Some of them were captured. And I think that after that there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You're being asked about events when Albanians or people from Albania were dressed in VJ uniforms, masquerading as VJ soldiers, and it's about that I would like a specific example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can't give you an example. But I don't think that these people who were crossing the border with weapons in 1998, that they actually wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it sounds as though the witness has misunderstood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I was asking you about some information you gave during the Milosevic trial where you said you had reports that people were coming across the border from Albania, probably Kosovo Albanians, I'm not sure, that those people would dress in VJ uniforms, that they spoke the Serbian language, and that they committed several crimes. What I wondered is if you were ever able to verify any of that information that you told the Court in Milosevic that you had received through your security organs.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Such information reached us through the chain of command. The commanders reported on those events in the areas of their responsibility. They took appropriate measures. And the security organs had no special jurisdiction over that because we're talking about combat activities, combat actions. We knew about the existence of some centres from which these people were brought in, where they were train, and through our channels we received information about possible axes of their infiltration, even sometimes the time when that would happen, and then the units in the field, combat units, took appropriate combat action to deal with that ambushes and so on. But to be quite specific, this went or should have gone through the reporting line up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Farkas, can you give us a specific example of an occasion when this happened now that you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't. I would have to go through those combat reports. So I really can't recall that. This happened quite often. I can't recall a specific example now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, earlier today when you were being questioned by lawyer Visnjic there were quite a few questions about crimes being committed in Kosovo in 1999 and the reporting system regarding those crimes, and the general impression that -- that I think came from your testimony was that there was a regimen of punishment and prosecution that was working well, but there was a reporting problem so that that information wasn't making its way up to the Supreme Command and up to the commanding general, and that -- I'm curious about that because of some testimony you gave in Milosevic. And now I'm at page 46315 of the Milosevic transcript. What you said in that case was that: "Reports of crimes came up through the chain of command through the security channels, so as soon as we heard of such things measures were taken in order to punish the perpetrators." So apparently those reports actually were coming up through the security channels and you were learning of them as that went on. Is that what you were saying in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I said that the security organs at certain levels did their work because these crimes were committed in the field and those people, those security organs, they detected that, and then from the brigade up to the corps and army level measures were taken by competent organs to detect those crimes, identify perpetrators and prosecute them. The Supreme Command Staff did not get the information, detailed enough information of an appropriate scope because the actions were going on not only in Kosovo but throughout the whole territory, and the Chief of the General Staff should have been informed about the events, particularly from the area where the fighting was the fiercest. So if I did say that, I did say in that sense the security organs, together with the commands because they were part of the commands and staffs and so on, dealt with that. And they did prosecute many of those cases. I was able to learn that when I went down there during the war, but because of the reporting and taking appropriate measures and in order to bolster the judicial organs and so on, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff was not in a position to take appropriate measures because he did not get enough information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any crimes that were reported up through those channels as to which no action was taken against perpetrators that were identified or those crimes were simply ignored? Do you know if that happened?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I got the information after our visits. Then we would get more detailed documents and information about the judicial proceedings. Those documents existed and cases were being prosecuted, but those events -- information about those events did not reach us. So there was a bottleneck in the flow of information from the level of the army to the Supreme Command Staff. There was an obstruction. They completed their job. They prosecuted their -- those cases, and they felt that this was enough, and they did not report further up the chain of command. That's the impression that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what we keep hearing, General, and I'd like to explore that just a little bit. You told us that you went to Kosovo to look into these matters in early May. I think you said around the 1st of May. Now, considering the war started on the 24th of March, you started getting that information apparently sometime in April, and that's when General Ojdanic decided that you should go to Kosovo and look into it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of any meeting that General Ojdanic had had with General Pavkovic, General Lukic and Mr. Milosevic on the 4th of May? Did you ever know anything about that meeting if it happened?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I really don't know about the existence of any such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you think you went to Kosovo before that date, the 4th of May, or after?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I think it was after that. I went to Kosovo -- I spent two days there, and I came back on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: And I spent only two days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you went to Kosovo, when did you first see General Pavkovic? Did you see him when you immediately got there or when you were getting ready to come back? When was it you met with him?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I couldn't recall at this point in time, but it seems to me that it was when I was getting ready to go back. That's where we met, because he was in the field with his security chief, so that even his security chief was not present. I did not contact him while I was down there. And when he came back, we met very briefly. I was already practically on my way back. I was already heading out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it you informed General Pavkovic of your findings that the crimes were being properly detected and prosecuted but the reporting was not adequate. I assume you told him that.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: It seems to me that we met very briefly. There was very fierce action. At that time I stated the reason for my arrival that I was duty-bound to give him, and I presented to him the problem, that the problem was that we were not getting enough information and crimes were being committed, and I was not sure that they were managing to deal with all of it. I told him that there was this problem and that there was this communication problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- the communication problem was -- was what? What -- what level was it that was failing to report? Was it the security people that were failing to send reports up through security channels?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the reporting channels went from one security organ to the other. I said that they were integral parts of the commands. And in all of the reports that were drafted at a certain level to the superior command, they took part in writing the report, and they put what they had learned into this report. So you have of to differentiate between different levels. So they stated that there was an incident. The military police carried out the on-site investigation. The courts then took over. But there were some problems at certain levels causing these reports not to reach us at the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that at the beginning the war General Pavkovic ordered the -- the prosecutors and the military courts in the 3rd Army area to provide him with daily reports regarding their activities? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of those orders of the lower commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware that virtually every --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: It is quite possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You wanted to finish that answer, so please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, when the war started war courts were set up, and they were under the jurisdiction of the army command and then in the units lower down. And the judicial organs were in contact with the commands, and whatever the commands uncovered they would do their job. Now, whether it would be the security organs or the command, they would do their job and then they would transfer that to the courts, and they did their job as independent organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, are you aware that virtually every day General Pavkovic in his daily combat report to the General Staff included a paragraph on the activities of the military prosecutor and the military courts? Are you aware that have? Did you see those reports?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I did not see anything of that kind because I was not there. General Gajic was there, and the daily combat reports, regular or extraordinary, were sent to him. And had he reached -- had he gotten any such reports, he was duty-bound to inform me about those reports, but he never did. That information never reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's very easy to check that, whether there were really such elements in those daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, they'll be seen by the Judges in this case, I can assure you of that. The -- I think what you're now telling us, if General Gajic was getting this information, it was his fault for not telling you about it. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, that's not what I meant. Had such information reached General Gajic, he would have informed me, and he would have submitted that to me. So they did not reach him. And you can check that fairly easily through those daily reports that were sent in. That's not a problem. You have everything. You have those daily operational reports, and it is very easy to see, and there's no need for me now to strain and try to remember something that really didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I totally agree with you, and the Judges -- the Judges will see those reports. Now, you went to Kosovo in early May, returned on the 7th, and I take it immediately told General Ojdanic what it was you had learned while you were there.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I informed him briefly orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then tell me the next thing that happened. Was the meetings -- were the meetings on the 16th and 17th with General Pavkovic and Milosevic, were those the next thing that happened or did Vasiljevic and Gajic go to Kosovo before those meetings?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This involves several question, doesn't it. The first one, a reaction did follow on the part of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff to take measures straight away, to establish what happened, and to see what it was that I had learned. It so happened that in that period the deputy chief of the army department was in Belgrade on some private business, and in that period between the 16th and my return our documents were reviewed and talks were held with Djuric. I think his name was Djuric. Colonel Djuric. And this further amplified this information before the meeting of the 16th. Then the meeting took place on the 16th when General Pavkovic confirmed all of this and added some other elements too. These were things that we had not been aware of before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So additional information was developed between your return from Kosovo on the 7th and when General Pavkovic came to Belgrade to report on the 16th, and we've already heard a lot about what General Pavkovic's report was about on that date and the meeting the next day with Milosevic where he basically repeated that report. And I'm trying to hurry here, General, because I'm using more time than I said I would. And he repeated that report, and it wouldn't have come then, I take it, as any surprise to you or General Pavkovic if General Pavkovic sent an additional report on the 25th of May saying that there's a problems with crimes being committed here in Kosovo. That wouldn't have been any surprise to anybody because you'd already had several reports about it, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't have any reports in writing. There were no written reports. This came after all the measures taken, then my stay down there, then the meeting on the 16th, then the meeting at Milosevic's. So this came as a product, this particular information. If it exists in writing, I've never seen it. If it does exist, then it came after all of these measures that were ordered by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really don't understand what you're telling us now. Are you saying that the only information you had was what you learned when you did your investigation and what you were told by General Pavkovic, and because none of it was in writing that you didn't any obligation to deal with it in any way?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, as for these problems, it is lower the commands and organs that dealt with them, and this is shown by the fact that they prosecuted many of the cases that they uncovered. The problem is that we did not get anything in writing from the army command, not even in a summarised version or not even information of any other kind until what we did. All of this was happening on the 25th of May. And this is written information coming from the level of the army command. Well, if that existed, I did not see that. If it does exist, then it is a product of all the measures that were taken beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You were shown during your direct testimony 3D493, and you probably still have it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, is identical to 3D479, which I indicated that I would use but I might as well use the same one lawyer Visnjic used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were referred to page 1 in English at the bottom where it has the language: "There are problems involving humanitarian crime." Now, this is a report that you're making to the Supreme Command chief of staff. You talk about this full analysis having been made by ZNUB. You say most of the atrocities have been documented and are currently before the military court's organs, the kinds of crimes, and you say around 95 per cent have been arrested and under investigation. Now, I take it you were being quite honest in your report on that date as to what your investigation had shown; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: It's not my investigation. This investigation was conducted by lower-level commands and units and courts. That is the result of all of those reports that had arrived until that point in time about cases that were prosecuted and cases that were learned about. That is to say that the security organs and commands learned about. As for all of these cases that were learned about, 95 per cent were prosecuted. That is not to say that all crimes and criminal offences that had taken place were uncovered. What is referred to here are those where proceedings were initiated. Some were still in the pre-investigation stage or the investigation stage. And, sir, that is the 76th day of the war, that is to say the last days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions for you. You discovered these reporting problems between the 6th and 7th of May while you were down there in Kosovo, and I take it those reporting problems ended at that point, that, you know, as a general that you ordered them to report properly and after that point there were no more reporting problems, after the 7th of May, true?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: You didn't understand me correctly. These reports are a command matter. Commanders can issue orders, send these combat reports through regular channels. I just indicated that there was a problem and that it should be resolved, and then the commands and commanders of the corps and armies were duty-bound to overcome this problem and inform the command. I did not have the right to issue orders to units and commands. I just viewed the problem from a professional point of view, and I pointed out the problem, just as an artillery man would, just as an engineering officer would when he toured an area and realised that there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so when you reported this to General Ojdanic after your return, like on maybe the 8th of May or something, did you see an order that he issued regarding better reports, the requirement of better reports? I'm trying to find out if that problem was solved rather immediately upon your report of it, and if not, why not.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: This problem, if it had been resolved and how it had been resolved, well, it was resolved in some way or it started being resolved only after the 16th, after the direct meeting and the briefing of the chief -- or, rather, the commander of the 3rd Army. In the interim, I don't know. Perhaps General Pavkovic, on the basis of this brief meeting, blitz meeting we had, he collected data in order to compile a report, and that is what he might have used to report to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff and to President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This meeting that you had where you made your report to the Supreme Command chief of staff at 3D4693, that was on the 8th of June. That's over a month from the time you came back from Kosovo. And it's also just a couple of days before withdrawal of all forces from Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, no. I first reported -- I mean, after my return, sometime around the 7th, I reported to the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, and after that what followed was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm talking about this specific document, 3D493. It is dated the 8th of June, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was very shortly before the withdrawal of -- of all forces from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The question that I have about that is did UNMIK cooperate with your security forces, your investigators, to continue investigation of these crimes, to allow you into Kosovo to interview witnesses, victims of rape or persons who had seen crimes committed? Were you able to continue your investigation after the forces left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We were not able to. We had no rights of access. I think that is the case even up to the present day. There is no possibility of reconstructing certain things, investigating, and so on. UNMIK entered, the forces entered, and only the terrorist organisations remained, and within UNMIK later turn into the armed force of that territory. So we had no possibilities. Civilian ones either, I think, but the military had no way of having access and continuing to resolve of the problems that they started dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know of any efforts made to try to get cooperation from UNMIK to assist with these continuing investigations, or was it simply a situation where you were without witnesses basically?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Attempts were made. I believe that to this day attempts are being made to have these matters resolved. However, to the best of my knowledge we had not had any access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And my last question. You talked about General Pavkovic at the meetings in Belgrade on the 16th and 17th recommending that there be a commission to investigate all of the issues that were raised in these meetings, the subordination issues, the crime issues, all of these issues, and Mr. Sainovic agreed with him that that was a good idea. What I'm wondering is if you know why that didn't happen. Why didn't Mr. Milosevic approve that and set it in motion? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: First of all, I wasn't the one who proposed that, the establishment of that commission. It was Mr. Pavkovic who proposed that at that briefing at Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... But my question is do you know why Mr. -- General Pavkovic's proposal was not adopted by Milosevic and put into motion? Why didn't he do that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: First of all, previously a few things had been said that had to be done. First of all, the president decidedly order that had para-police forces withdraw. Arkan, the Wolves, Boca, et cetera, that the problems be resolved with these para-police units first of all. And once this is dealt with and certain measures are taken, then and meeting should take place between the MUP and the military and then we should raise the question of the right order and way of resolving these problems. That problem was put in very strong terms. The president said that this kind of lack of cooperation and this kind of attitude equalled sabotage. And this was a reprimand to me and Rade Markovic. And he explicitly first gave an order to the MUP that they resolve the question of these para-police forces and then Rade Markovic said that this was underway and that these units would be withdrawn and measures would be taken and only after that this meeting was supposed to take place which did not take place because the sequence of events was a very fast one and very soon there was the withdrawal from that territory, but there was this initiative vis-a-vis the MUP from my side specifically. We did try to schedule that kind of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you don't -- I take it the answer is you don't know were Milosevic didn't set up this commission that Pavkovic suggested and Sainovic thought was a good idea, do you?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's not that Milosevic was supposed to organise that.
