Milosevic said, first of all, the police should resolve their internal problems with these para-organisations and we should meet and we should set up a commission and then we should find the right way and make proposals to resolve this. However, this did not happen for the above-mentioned reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was for the state, and I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. -- Or, rather, General, may I introduce myself. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence attorneys for General Vladimir Lazarevic and one of the first things I wish to do is to wish you a good day.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, let me ask you a couple of questions to clear some things up. Today in your evidence you said that you were the assistant to the Federal Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now I want to know whether the units of the Civilian Defence and civilian protection in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and throughout the territory it of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were under the federal defence ministry. They were subordinate to them?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, in organisational terms they were part of and subordinate to the Federal Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that the Ministry of Defence pursuant to the constitution and the law on defence and other bylaws provided weapons for all its units of the Civilian Defence?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're on the topic of the civilian defence, could you please tell me if you remember how many people were in the civilian defence in Kosovo Metohija in that period 1998, beginning of 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, according to the establishment that was made and approved for the civilian defence and the civilian protection, the communication units and encryption units that were all within the jurisdiction of the Federal Ministry of Defence in Kosovo there were about 9.000 personnel there. In accordance with the establishment, in accordance with the criteria that were used in order to produce the establishment. Over 9.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do you know that there was an administration for the defence of Pristina and that it had its own warning and surveillance centre?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That administration, in accordance with systematisation of the civilian structures existed throughout the territory of Yugoslavia as it was then. There were such centres in Vojvodina and so on all over the territory. There were such centres not only as part of those administrations but also in lower organisational units wherever it was deemed that there could be some threat from chemical accidents, adverse weather, natural disasters, and those surveillance and warning centres were set up in such locations and that also applied in the war, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, let me just follow up. Do you know that those administrations that you just described to us sent their reports using their own reporting channels to the federal defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, no. There was a hierarchy, just as it existed in the army. So if we're talking about the Pristina administration, they were duty-bound to send their reports up to the branch organ in Serbia which was an organisational unit covering the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And this republican organ in Serbia would then send -- send this report further up to the federal defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The reports, the documents that it deemed to be necessary for dealing with some problems or that were something that the federal ministry of defence should deal with were sent up to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the General please be shown Exhibit P1294.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in this Prosecution exhibit there is your signature. Could you tell us briefly, really very briefly, that the appointment of the commanders of the civilian defence staffs were done by you, that that was not part of the system of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. As the assistant for the federal defence minister for civilian defence, it was within my purview to make such appointments, and I was supposed to update all those documents regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you mentioned Izbica. I'm going to ask you one question. Do you know, do you recall, do you have that in your memory, clear in your memory, that the exhumation and all the other investigative actions at the mass grave in Izbica were carried out by civilian investigating organs of the District Court in Kosovska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters kindly ask for all the microphones to be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the information that I got from my assistant upon his return from Kosovo on the 7th, I got the information and indeed the impression that they did that together, that military organs and civilian organs were present there while those activities were carried out. I don't know any details. I know that the mass grave was exhumed and that post-mortem examinations of the dead bodies were carried out and that the reports -- I don't have any further knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, am I right if I say that if the military investigative organs took part together with the civilian organs and that they determined -- and determined that the army had not taken part in that incident, would then they have to file a report and whether they had taken appropriate measures in that case by referring the case for further action by the civilian organs?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I can't really give you a proper answer to that question because I myself am not certain at all about this oral report that General Vasiljevic gave. I can't really be certain that the military organs really had participated in that. That's how it seems to me now. That's how I recall that, that they went there together to that area and that the exhumation was carried out jointly. Now as for the second part of your question about the jurisdiction, I think that it happened at the end of the war, and the judicial organs were supposed to decide on the jurisdiction. The judicial organs, both military and civilians, had to decide about the jurisdiction over those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you perhaps mean to say that the military organs took part in the exhumation, because in that team that carried out the exhumation, there was an expert pathologist or forensic medical expert, Dr. Tomasevic, from the Military Medical Academy upon the order of the District Court in Kosovska Mitrovica. That was a civilian court, in other words.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know of those details. I don't know about the jurisdictions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Thank you very much, General. Let me just ask you for some clarification. At page 41, line 19 of the transcript today, you mentioned the name Colonel Djuric, deputy chief security -- chief of security. General, in that case are we maybe talking about Lieutenant Colonel Stevan Djurovic, the deputy of the security organ in the Pristina Corps, who on the 8th of May, 1999, informed your deputy, General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, about the crimes that had been prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man I was talking about. I would like to apologise both to you and both to him for my faulty memory, for being unable to give you the correct name. He was there in a private capacity because of some family issues, and this fact was used to get some more details about what I had learned while I was there in Kosovo, but that was done by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp. Sorry, you didn't -- was there an indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We raised our hand and we also sent the information regarding our estimate to the court officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we should break at this stage before we start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will break at this stage, and that break will be 20 minutes. So we'll resume at 10 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Farkas, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic on behalf of Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, General. As you've heard I'm one of the lawyers for Mr. Sreten Lukic in this case. Now I'm going to be asking you several questions and I'm going to be going through some documents but I'm using the documents just to be fair to you and to give you all the information upon which my questions are based, so please unless my -- wait for my question to see what if anything you need to review in the documents to refresh your recollection that way we'll move much smoother. Now, my colleague had asked you about the Civilni Zastita, the Civilian Protection Units. I would like to confirm with you sir that in fact these units of the Civilni Zastita wore blue uniforms with a yellow emblem of some sort.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the uniform worn by the civilian protection in accordance with international regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... To the next topic. You mentioned three groups affiliated with the MUP. I believe you called them para-police. I'd like to first start with the group known as the Boca Medic group and the question will be very simple if you just listen all the way through the end without looking at the documents until we get to the actual question. 3D1055 is a document that should be there and available for you if you need it. This is the 13 May 1999 information issued by your service regarding this -- in here it's listed a paramilitary today I guess you would call it a para-police based on your testimony group led by Boca Medic, talks of a crime they committed at the end of March in Podujevo and they were driven out of Kosovo by the commander of 354th brigade of the VJ. Now, two other documents that I sent there for you to have if need be are 6D1135 and 4D00371 and these are the Pristina Corps regular combat reports from the 31st of March, 1999, and the 1st of April, 1999 respectively it. I will save you the trouble of reading through those since they are lengthy documents. Neither one of those documents references the Podujevo incident involving the Medic group and the conduct of the commander of the 354th brigade of the VJ. Now, the question I have for you, would you expect that such a drastic event would in fact be reflected in the combat reports if it happened in a manner set forth in your is security organ's information, particularly the involvement of the commander of the 354th Brigade of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know how the reporting system functioned in its entirety and these are documents from the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, the Pristina Corps to send to the army command. I guess they should be entered or marked, but as for those events of the 17th of March, Mr. Rade Markovic talked about them and he confirmed that those units were there and that they committed crimes, that they were disbanded or expelled out of this area. That's what Mr. Rade Markovic said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: On the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The May I think?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, the 17th of May. But regardless of all that, this should being mentioned in those reports but that's not important because he confirmed that those units existed and that they had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Expelled from those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. I had to pause for the translation and the transcript to catch up with us. We'll get to the 17th May meeting and what I want to draw out of it. What I'm trying to figure out now is to find out the reliability and veracity of the information that your service had at the time. Now, am I correct that had the 354th Brigade of the VJ been involved in the Podujevo incident your security organs in the field would have known about this incident shortly after it occurred on the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Every unit, including this brigade that you mentioned, has its security organ, and as I explained the security organ is a part of the command system. Whatever the commanders do at the briefings, whatever they say there, the security organ is aware of that and he takes part in drafting the report that is sent to the superior command. The answer to your question is that the staff or the command of that unit had to know, and that includes the security organ. They had to know about any events.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, given that the first information from your security organisation came on the 13th of May, almost two months after the incident in question, and given that it came -- strike that. If the organs had to have known of the incident if it involved the commander, how do you explain the fact that this information is written almost two months later, on the 13th of May? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the only explanation is that the information about this incident did not reach the Supreme Command Staff through the regular chain of command and chain of reporting. So they were solving a problem. They solved it the way they did and they failed to report on that. And the information about Boca and so on, this is something that we got in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, we had Mr. Stoparic, a member of this reserve SAJ unit and a former Scorpion who was there that day testify that in fact it was the police SAJ commanders who ordered his group out of Kosovo. Given the foregoing things that we've gone through, do you concede the possibility that in fact the 13 May information, as presented by your security organ, did not give the complete and full picture, particularly in regards to the participation of the commander of the 354th Brigade of the VJ who in fact is not mentioned by Mr. Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible. I didn't get the reports about the events, but this information from the security administration talks about the existence of this group there, and we are, I think, relaying this information to, I think, MUP too. And later on at that meeting Rade Markovic himself said that such groups existed, that they had been there, they went away, and then they came back. So that's the information that I am aware of. That's what Rade Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Reported to the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The question I want to ask you is isn't it correct that --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- The first date, this May 13th, 1999, that your service finally writes something about the Boca Medic group occurs after the RDB, and specifically the person in Rade Markovic, went to President Milosevic and exposed the Pauk saboteur group going behind your back? [Interpretation] Well, it may be easier to ask the question in Serbian because I see that there is a problem with interpretation. General, is it true that your information related to Boca Medic group of the 13th of May, 1999, that this information happened after, that the RDB of MUP and their leadership, Rade Markovic, went behind your back to report to Milosevic about the existence of Pauk group within the army?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't understand the question. What do you mean going behind my back? The existence of Pauk group. I really don't know. What do you mean when you say they went behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Well, sir, those are the words used by Aleksandar Vasiljevic your subordinate used in this courtroom you'll have to ask him, but if you don't know I'll move on. Now, a question I would have for you regarding this topic is why if according to document 6D998, which should also be there for your review, it's a short document, you could probably read it rather quickly. This is a supplemental information relating to Boca Medic's people that is dated the 16th of May, 1999, wherein it is stated that these -- this group was a lawful MUP organ that in fact had been sent -- ordered to Kosovo by General Rodza of the MUP and General Gajic explained this was General Rodza Djordjevic. If -- and that's 6988, I'm sorry. If as of the 15th of May, 1999, you knew that this group had official status within the MUP, wore MUP uniforms, had documentation showing them to be reservist MUP and had been tasked in the field by the deputy minister of interior Djordjevic, why is it that your organs and your subordinates and even you today even to this date keep referring to them as either paramilitary or para-police? How can that fit your description of paramilitary or para-police?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know under whose command he was part of, what unit he was. I can repeat only one thing that I know I'm 100 per cent sure. These people who were present there, they were told to us about by Mr. Rade Markovic. I didn't see this document. I don't know what this means. If they were, then they were, but the fact is that they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Prove [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please not overlap with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Rade Markovic say they were not reservists of the MUP on one hand as far as Boca Medic is concerned and the RDB reservists when this comes to Arkan's men?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, that's not what he said. They said that both had committed crimes and Arkan had offered 100 people to him and he accepted 30 people and I really can't see who this Arkan was when he was able to just offer those people like that. The police had its own regular way of mobilising people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: And mobilising its reserve force, and it was said at that meeting in fact that both MUP and the RDB, I guess, had regulations in place for that. It was impossible for Arkan to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Just come and say I have 100 people if you want them. Well, fine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... If you can just finish up with these Boca Medic group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it keeps going off by itself, maybe, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, so we finish off this Boca Medic group, in May of 1999 when you drafted your initial information in -- and then the supplemental information and participated in the 17th May meeting where Rade Markovic was present, at that time did your service know anything about the alleged crimes committed in 1995 in Locina by individuals affiliated with group of Boca Medic the so-called Scorpion video that first aired long after the Kosovo conflict and was made public during the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- In May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, at that time I was not in service. At that time I was the assistant defence minister for civilian defence. So I really had no knowledge of that. I didn't get any information in my official capacity or in fact in any other capacity of the existence of this group. That was a long time ago when I was not in service so --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you about May 1999, General. Did you at that time, you or your service, have information about this videotape and the crimes committed by those units in Locina area in Bosna?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Apart from what we wrote down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm showing you the documents to show you that I'm not running away from anything that's written on paper, sir. Now, with respect to the negative image and reputation of the so-called Scorpions, that really arose after the Scorpion video was shown some time in the 2000s, long after the Kosovo conflict. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. At that time when this information was written and when the meeting was held with Slobodan Milosevic, I did not know that they were called the Scorpions, I think. It may have been mentioned, but in this information we say that allegedly they're called the Scorpions, and the other ones were called the Tigers and so on. So these names did not mean anything to us at the time. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, if we can move on to another group that you mentioned and that your colleagues also mentioned, the Wolves of the Drina, "Vokovi Sa Drine." Did anyone mention this unit at the 17 May 1999 meeting with Slobodan Milosevic and, if so, who?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I think I cannot remember exactly that anyone mentioned this. It was only Boca's group that was being mentioned as such and the Tigers. I did not remember that the Wolves were mentioned by anyone present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, am I correct that as records these "Vokovi Sa Drine," Wolves of the Drina, your service did not have any information as to where they were based or who sent them to Kosovo Metohija allegedly?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We did not have any exact information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the information you did have was rather scant?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, probably so because we are not in charge of such organs. If some groups appear without being identified, then we cooperate with the MUP. We give them information in order to resolve who they are. We establish that they were not members of the military, Boca's group, that they were not Tigers, and then it was dealt with in the field who was who. They were members of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Boca's for example and Arkan's Tigers and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please wait for the interpretation of the witness's answer to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you will have to wait until the interpretation is complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I promise you, sir, we're going to work through each one of these groups. So please bear with me and you'll have your say on each of these groups in due turn. To your knowledge did your service issue any written reports or did anyone else in the army mention these Wolves of the Drina in combat reports like we saw for Boca Medic's group?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of any such information coming to the Supreme Command Staff all the way up until my team came, rather, Aco Vasiljevic, who I think was the first one to hear of the names of these groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, both of your -- your colleagues, General Gajic in particular, reported that the commander of this group, the Wolves the Drina, was a certain individual named Karisek nicknamed Legenda. Karisek nicknamed Legenda. Do you recall from what source you got about this from the commander was it the same source in Bosnia who gave you the initial information about this formation?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I did not deal with that, with those sources of information. Quite simply they were not within my purview. Generally speaking, I did not deal with them at all. I was just supposed to inform the MUP that we had such knowledge and they should resolve it in the field. So I did not investigate that. It wasn't for the chief of security of the army of Yugoslavia to investigate some units that were down there in that territory and that belonged to the police or the SDB. However, if they commit some crimes and if we find out about that, well, then that would be stated in stronger terms and then we would be duty-bound vis-a-vis the MUP just as they were vis-a-vis us to inform them or they inform us about crimes that were being committed by units in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I see. And your obligations and duties were effectuated by informing the MUP two months after it arrested the people and had already processed them about the Boca Medic group existing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, I provided the information. Had I received this information, I would have provided it straight away. We got this information. We informed them, and they said, "We know, and we have completed the job. Thank you for having told us, but we finished this." I don't see anything strange about that. We provide information at the moment we find out about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you say that it was not your -- within your purview to deal with such matters, but yet both of your immediate subordinates dealt with these matters almost exclusively. So I want to know whether in fact you know if the source for the information about the Wolves of the Drina and about this Legenda, Nedeljko Karisek, that General Gajic talked about whether the source was considered authentic and reliable.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That is not correct. That is not correct that my deputies were dealing with those problems exclusively. As they were in the field in contact with security organs, they found out about these things and they provided the kind of information they did. We provided this information to the MUP. As for investigations, where they came from and why they came, we didn't deal with that. They said what they said. So it's not that my organs were supposed to deal with that. We did not at all investigate what the MUP was doing with those units. Once we received information, then we would pass it on and clear things up that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well surely, sir, your service had a means for determining whether the information it received was credible and came from an authenticated source. Was this information about the Wolves of the Drina that General Gajic testified about vetted so that the source was considered to be reliable and authenticated according to all your resources?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the checks will be done by those who provided information, but we checked and we realise it did not come from our own ranks. And then we expected that the MUP organs would check where they came from and what they did. So really these questions, I don't understand what you're trying to achieve. These people found out in the field that there were some groups messing about in uniform and immediately they provided information about this as soon as they found out, as soon as I found out, and so on and so forth. Later on they checked. Why would they expel Boca if he was good, and that group?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, General Gajic indicated that the source was from Bosnia, not from the ground in Kosovo for this Wolves of the Drina group. Now the reason I'm asking these questions is very simple and I think the only way to do is to just to present you with the documentation. Now, according to the documents in our possession and I'm go through it with you document by document in a second. Just listen to the beginning portion of the question. According to our information, during the Bosnian conflict the Wolves of the Drina were not a paramilitary but were a specialised unit of the Drina corps and the Zvornik Brigade of the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, and they were commanded by a professional army officer, Milan Jolovic, nicknamed Legenda. Now, the documents that you should have in front of you, sir, except for the first one which is only available in English that support this and identically refer to both the unit and the commander being this Jolovic, are 601136, a November 6, 1995, news article including an interview with Mr. Jolovic from Vreme; 601138, the statement of facts presented by Dragan Obrenovic and the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal in support -- that's also in English, in support of a guilty plea before the United Nations Tribunal; 6D1137, which should be in front of you in Serbia, a command order of the Drina Corps to the Bratunac Brigade dated 2 June 1995 again references the Wolves of the Drina and their commander Legenda Jolovic; and also two witnesses that are -- that testified under oath in the Popovic case here in recent history at transcript page 8871, lines 6 through 8, transcript page 2667, line 23 through transcript page 2668, line 3. All these sources explicitly refer to the Wolves of the Drina as a unit within the army of the Republika Srpska under the command of Captain First Class at that time Milan Jolovic, a professional army officer who by the way in case you don't have that information just retired as commander of the army of Yugoslavia's 72nd Special Brigade a few months ago. Now -- I have to wait for the transcript to catch up with us. First of all -- now, am I correct --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: First of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... So please bear with me. I only have two more questions on this point and I'll move on, and we're almost done. First of all, am I correct that elements of the 72nd Special Brigade of the VJ were deployed in Kosovo Metohija in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: First of all, as for all of these documents that you mentioned, I don't have any of them here. First and foremost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, General, please answer the question you've been asked for now. I hope we're going to come back to the documents in a moment but just answer the question counsel has asked you which has nothing on the face of it to do with the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of that, of any units, entities, and so on in 1999 existing in the territory of Kosovo, in the establishment, in the formations of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters could not hear the speaker from counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've missed the question again. I accept what you're thinking this is a very confusing way of going about it. You've been asked whether it's correct that elements of the 72nd Special Brigade of the VJ were deployed in Kosovo in 1999. Now, you should be able to answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could return to this -- these documents. One thing that is clear from these documents is that they conflict with the information that your service had about the Wolves of the Drina. I do not need you to comment any further on what is contained in these documents, but I would like to ask you, given this information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I would like the witness to confirm that he has the documents, because in his question Mr. Ivetic says that something is clear in these documents. So for things to be clear to him should have the documents in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I for one am not appreciating this approach to cross-examination. I don't even know at the moment what the witness is claiming is his source of information about the Wolves of the Drina and you seem to be making certain assumptions about that. Now, what does he know about the source? I thought he said he didn't know what the source of the information was, but perhaps you'd like to clarify that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And depending on that answer all of this is argumentative and not appropriate cross-examination but that will become clear once we hear the answer to the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir -- now, sir, the Wolves of the Drina were such an important part of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's just ask the question, Mr. Ivetic. No more speeches for the moment. Straight to question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned the Wolves of the Drina, General. What knowledge do you have of them and the source for that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: During the stay of my team headed by Aco Vasiljevic in the territory of Kosovo through our organs of security of the units they heard that a group or formation under that name existed. That is to say these formations were in the field. The information came from the security organs of the army of Yugoslavia in the field. When we heard it from them, we did not check this any further. We informed the MUP, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then my follow-up, sir, is a question that I asked but I believe you did not answer. Since you do know the source of this information and what information was contained, did you consider the source or sources of this information to be verified and credible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic -- just, a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not have any need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this takes me back a bit. First of all, Mr. Ivetic asks the witness a few times one and the same question, but let's leave that aside. Then he asks the witness to speculate, and then if the witness speculates then he gives it back to him as a return information. So that's the way they've been dealing with this same topic for three or four times. I don't mind the General answering that, but I don't see that this is taking us anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Ivetic. There's nothing wrong with your question. The question was, General, did you consider the source or sources of your information to be verified and credible, and you had begun to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not think it was necessary for me to look at the credibility or incredibility of that information received from security organs of the army of Yugoslavia from that terrain, and it is this source information, this original information, that I sent further to the MUP without any further verifications or checks, and I'm not entitled to that. I concluded that it was not from our formation, from our jurisdiction, and as soon as we learned about this we sent this information on to those who were in charge of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Was the information that was sent to the MUP in written form, and where can that be found?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, if they were in writing, then they can be found in the archives of the security administration. At this moment I don't know. If they got this in the field they could have quite simply asked Aco Vasiljevic and any organ could have come to some MUP commander or the authorised official and say orally, well, look there is something going on here and see what this is all about. If there are written traces of this, official ones, then it could be found in the archives of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your question is not clear. Are you saying that the MUP don't have this in writing, or are you asking a question about whether it came to the VJ in writing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is related to some documents searches that we are in the process of trying to complete and thus far no such documents have been given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question relates to whether the MUP actually had this reported to them in writing by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the Wolves the Drina; correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Farkas, was that -- was any report made to the MUP that you're aware of about the presence of or activities of the Wolves of the Drina in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give an accurate answer to that question except for this report that we sent. I really cannot give an accurate answer whether there was anything in writing, a written report, communication between us at that level, that is to say the administration and the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you mean by "except for this report that we sent"? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it pertains to some information in relation to Boca Medic, that is, on the 13th of May. That is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's got nothing to do with the Wolves of the Drina, has it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm saying that apart from this written information, I can confirm that this exists, but I don't know about others, that there was that kind of communication in relation to the Wolves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Think I'll move on to my last is series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General you've been chomping at the bit to talk about the Arkanovci and the Rade Markovic's statements in the May 17th meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I think Mr. Ivetic is being carried away just a bit here. Chomping at the bit. I think it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the translation. I have no problems with that being taken out and we can move forward efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's withdrawn. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, General, first of all, is it correct that prior to the 17 May 1999 meeting where Rade Markovic was with President Milosevic your service had very little, if any, information regarding so-called Arkanovci in Kosovo Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know what you consider to be very little, if any. We have information there is a group in Kosovo called the Tigers and that they belong to Arkan's organisation. As far as we knew up until that time and that is what we reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And again you say that's what we reported. That's curious. Was it in written form? Because again with the Arkanovci we have thrust to find any written reports from your service giving the details. Where you report it to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I think that there are no written traces of communication between us and the MUP except for this meeting that you have been saying that I could hardly wait to come to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note could all other microphones be switched off while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We're getting a note from the interpreters to shut off microphones. I don't know if anyone else's is on apart from mine. I will turn it off when the witness answers just to make sure. Now, General, focusing on the 17th of May meeting, do you recall Rade Markovic mentioning that he had deployed 31 -- or excuse me 30 of 100 men offered by Arkan in uniforms of the JSO and that just prior to the meeting two of these individuals had killed an elderly couple and had been arrested and prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's not my witness but the question is very unclear. I don't know if it could be rephrased. I'm looking at the transcript here and I'm wondering if there might be a clear translation of the question having regard to what is written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Seems to me very specific about what was said at the meeting on the 17th of May. Well, it may seem inherently contradictory the question is clear enough. Can you help us with this, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, out in the field we received information from that -- or, rather, that some persons from that group had committed certain crimes. This is information from security organs. Later on at this meeting of the 17th it was clarified and Mr. Rade Markovic said what he said. I don't want to repeat all of that. From 100 and then 30 and then this crime was committed and they were arrested. This knowledge about the arrest of those two, that is what I learned on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note we cannot hear the speaker via videolink when anybody's microphone is on in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this crime committed by two individuals is the only evidence or information that your service had of crimes committed by these so-called Arkan's people. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I got at that meeting and it was defined that they were to be dealt with by the MUP and it was all supposed to be done in the spirit of President Milosevic's order, what did he say to process things, clear things up, Boca and the Wolves and everybody else, to clear up all these units that are or are not within the composition and how they are within the composition of the MUP, to get rid of them from the area of Kosovo and that they should not appear there. In relation to this, he also said the following: That the border should be closed and if necessary even the border towards the Drina should be closed so that we would not have individuals or units coming from there who would then do evil things in the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last question. You said within the composition of the MUP. Focusing on the Arkanovci, was it said that they were under the composition of the RJB or the RDB of the MUP, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, this is what was said, that Rade Markovic said that Arkan personally offered to him 100 persons, 100 of his young men, and that from that 100 he accepted 30, and he knew that those 30 committed some crimes, killed a few people there. So he himself said that. I am not inventing who it was that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question? Was it said that they were under the composition of the RJB or the RDB of the MUP? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what to answer yes or no to. I have to say what -- in what composition they were, what they were part of. According to what Rade Markovic said, they were part of the state security. Since Arkan had offered that to him and he had accepted it, and that leads me to believe that they were units that were part -- that belonged to the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, General. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp, where do we stand do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think since we have to take a 20-minute break, it will probably go over into tomorrow. I could try, but I don't think it's likely that we'd complete today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can the interpreters let me know if they would be willing to resume at quarter past 6.00? THE INTERPRETERS: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll have a shorter than normal break just now and we will resume at 6.15.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said in evidence that after your visit to Kosovo on the 6th, 7th May 1999, you discovered that there were quite a lot of crimes, serious crimes being committed in Kosovo, but that these crimes were not being reported up to the Supreme Command or to the Supreme Command Staff. What I'd like you to tell us is exactly where was the failure of reporting? Who was it who was supposed to report who did not report?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: In the chain of command it is quite clearly defined. The brigade commands, the corps command, the army command, and the competent strategic formations are the army commands that are supposed to report and communicate with the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So can I take it from your answer is that you are saying that it was the 3rd Army command that failed to report up about these crimes that you discovered were being perpetrated in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a failure there, but they had no failures in terms of prosecuting those responsible, but they had failed to report what they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So they failed to report the fact that these crimes were committed, and they failed to report what they had done in respect to these crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. More or less that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the security administration that you headed also had a security section in the 3rd Army that reported directly to you. Did that security sector --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No. They were also part of the command system. So they were to report to the subordinate army commander. They were the section, the chief of the section was a member of the army commander's staff, and all the reports that had come in were supposed to be integrated and security problems were to be flagged in those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In March of 1999, who was the head of the security sector in the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I think it was Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did not -- who was the head of the Pristina Corps security sector?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Momir Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So who was the head the 3rd Corps security sector -- 3rd Army, I beg your pardon, security sector?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, Momir Stojanovic was the head of the security, was the chief of the security in the 3rd Army in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Anyway, the question is this: Do you not know -- do you not know that Momir Stojanovic sent reports, that is security service reports, directly to the security administration in Belgrade during March or April?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Some reports were sent directly, and it is quite well-known which reports are to be sent directly, but again with the knowledge of the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, sorry. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems to me that the witness is not feeling well. That's why I got to my feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Farkas, are you able to carry on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I will be able to carry on for a little while longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much for assisting. Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Farkas, the evidence of General Gajic was that you, shortly after your appointment, you changed the system of reporting and caused both the Pristina Corps security sector and the 3rd Army security sector to report to you or to report to the security administration on a daily basis from March 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that is a completely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness answer first of all, then I'm hear from you. Just a moment. Please sit down. Please answer the question, Mr. Farkas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did change the system but not in the way that you say, that I or, rather, the security administration was to be informed. This was all directly integrated into the system of commands. It was in the chain of command. The brigades report to the corps, the corps reports to the army, and the army reports up the chain of command directly to the Supreme Command Staff and not the security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Stamp. Riaz, can you switch off the link just to my voice so that the general doesn't hear it. Thank you. Now, the reason, Mr. Cepic, I intervened there was we already have had evidence from the witness that the system changed at the start of the war, and the question wasn't framed in a way that was misleading to the point it would make it difficult for him to answer. He was able to answer and I was anxious that he should not be hearing what his answer should be from you. That is why I intervened and he has now answer the question in a fairly detailed way. That doesn't suggest he was mislead in any way He may have given evidence you don't like, I don't know; but there's nothing there to suggest that he was mislead..

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but the way the question was framed it was simply wrong. It was misstated by my learned colleague, Mr. Stamp, because at page 1, 5188, lines 1 through 9, General Gajic gave a reply that is consistent with the reply provided by General Farkas and the very point why I stood up, the reason why I did so, is because my learned colleague misquoted the question, and he's referring to something that was not stated, because General Gajic's evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't need to tell me something several times, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Stamp, what do you have to say about the inaccuracy of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not accept that what I represented was an inaccurate reproduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We don't need to resolve it at this stage. We'll move on to the next question. Please restore the link. Thank you for your patience, Mr. Farkas. We had to deal with a matter of law just now. We can now proceed with the evidence having dealt with that matter. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think you can answer this very quickly. So it is your evidence that the 3rd Army security sector did not have a responsibility to report up to the security administration in Belgrade on daily basis?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No, only in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- Exceptional circumstances and for everything else --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take it that if the bottleneck as you described it once, if the failure of reporting was at the level of the 3rd Army command, it was General Pavkovic who was failing to report to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, at the level of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: And the commander of the 3rd Army was Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown a document which I'll summarise just to be speedy. I won't show it to you unless you need to see it. This is 3D493 for the record. And that is a briefing that you had that you were present for at the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, General Ojdanic, dated the 8th of June. And in that document there is again a report by you about the failure of reporting up. That's the 8th of June. Was the problem of General Pavkovic's failure to report up that you discovered from the 5th to the 6th of June not resolved by the 8th of June? I beg your pardon. I'll withdraw the question. Was a problem that you discovered about the failure to report up at about the 5th to the 6th of May not resolved by the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, in a way it was resolved. The reports, regular reports, came in, I guess, but at this briefing, that's the last days of the war, there were technical problems and other problems related to reporting. So General Pavkovic cannot be the only one to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that your explanation as to why it is that this reporting problem arising from General Pavkovic's failure was not resolved after it was discovered after one month, is your last answer your explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, after the meeting, yes, it was resolved. And after the meeting with Mr. Milosevic some things were dealt with, some things were ordered, and for a while regular reports came in, but then again the problem cropped up when it came to the withdrawal of the troops from Kosovo, so that I really don't have an idea of the intensity of the reporting from the 3rd Army. I don't have anything very accurate, but I do have information that the information they were receiving were not sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I also refer to you another document that you were shown. This is 3D633, dated the 2nd of June, 1999, and this is what you said, this is a quote of you, and I'd like you to focus on the day as well 6th of June, 1999: "Crimes are being committed by all units in Kosovo. Reports on these acts are not going through regular channels and lines of command."

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And at page 3 you also said that: "Very little of what is contained in our combat reports indicates the negative phenomena," and you're talking about criminal activities. How is it that the problems in respect of reporting these crimes persisted up to the 2nd of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: After the meeting of the 17th, all the crimes that were committed and that were detected were dealt with, and then the chief of staff of the Supreme Command issued another order to the judicial organs to -- both to the courts and to the prosecutor's offices to assist and to produce an overview of all the cases that had been prosecuted to date. So that up to that moment everything had been cleared up and it was known what was prosecuted, what was not. That was in the report -- or, rather, I know that this report was made by the courts, but I don't know the details. So up until that date -- or as of that date all those problems were solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As of which date?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: But then when --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As of which date?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, as of the meeting of the 17th, because the order was issued at that day, and I don't know when the courts actually produced this report about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, how --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- The cases that were prosecuted, but there is this order of the chief of the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, you are saying that it was solved as of the meeting of the 17th of May, which is why I quoted what you said on the 2nd of June. How can you say it was solved on the 17th of May when on the 2nd of June you are reporting to the chief of General Staff the same problem?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Because a new situation happened because problems occurred once the forces began to pull out from the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: And there were problems involving the uncovering --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you. You said there were problems involving the uncovering of what?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, uncovering -- or reporting the uncovering the crimes, producing adequate documents about cases to be prosecuted, and at the same time parallel to that we had problems with the regrouping of the forces, the communication lines, but primarily the problems involved finding evidence and producing appropriate dossiers that the courts could use. We had the problems that we couldn't access those areas even at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 2nd of June. Which areas couldn't you access?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we're talking about, the 2nd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which areas couldn't you access then which affected your investigations?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Because the units were preparing for the pull-out, and they could not produce documents, valid documents, that could be used in court. We were in the territory at that time, but you know that you need certain preliminary investigative measures before an appropriate investigation is launched to produce a proper document. So there was knowledge, but it was impossible to produce appropriate, valid documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, did you -- General --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: They started --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, didn't you tell us in your testimony today that at the lower levels, brigade and below, the reporting and investigations were regular and proper, there were no problems with that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Therefore, General, what you're telling us now could not, I submit to you, be an explanation as to why there was still a problem with the reporting up of crimes and what was done in respect to the crimes by the 3rd Army command in June.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, there were no regular reports. There were the problems that I described, that valid evidence could not be produced of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, that, with respect, sorry, is not an answer to my question, but I'll move on for the sake of time. You mention the meeting on the 17th of June. Can I just ask you quickly -- thank you very much, Counsel. The meeting on the 17th of May. Persons from the -- well, one person from the MUP, Rade Markovic, and persons from the VJ were present, as well as the Supreme Commander, President Milosevic. Mr. Sainovic was also there. What was his role there?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: He was the deputy prime minister. I don't know in what capacity he was there, but in a way he was charged with monitoring the situation in Kosovo as the deputy prime minister. That's the impression that I had on the basis of what he said, what he proposed, what he -- the way he agreed to General Pavkovic's proposal to set up the state commission to deal with all those crimes and problems that occurred in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You're speaking about your impressions, so I'll move from there. General Vasiljevic said that after that meeting you and the remainder of those persons from the VJ left but left Rade Markovic and Mr. Sainovic with Mr. Milosevic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't recall who remained there. We, the generals, headed out because as soon as we got up General Ojdanic started issuing tasks to us even as we started walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know who stayed behind. I don't know where general and how general was able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we have a testimony, and I think including yours -- or may I just phrase the question this way: Is it not correct that after General Ojdanic received the reports from the security organs about the crimes in Kosovo, and he began receiving those reports, according to you, from early May 1999, that he made or issued orders as the concrete steps to be taken in investigating and prosecuting those crimes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it correct, is the evidence of some persons that have come here to testify on behalf of General Ojdanic correct that he issued orders to investigate and prosecute those responsible for crimes in Kosovo after he became aware of it in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's correct. He did issue orders and measures were taken beforehand and all orders were issued in order for those things not to be done, but after that meeting he issued orders to the courts, to the security service, to the military prosecutors' offices and to the commands of the strategic groups in the strictest possible terms that things -- measures should be taken to clear up all those crimes fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're also saying and I take it, this is the question, that there was no need for further measures, because although you discovered that crimes were being committed in Kosovo, the problem was that they were not being reported up. The 3rd Army was doing all that was necessary in respect of these crimes. If all that was to be done in respect to these crimes was to be done by the 3rd Army what was the need for the measures ordered by General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, there were problems, because then in addition to these activities there was ongoing mobilisation and demobilisation, and when we had over 13.000 men in that area, I think, new units came in and new commanders as well, this had to be dealt with. One had to put a stop to all of that. At the same time the judiciary and the Prosecution offices were supposed to intensify their work in terms of processing these crimes. So this need existed not only in the 3rd Army but in all armies. These orders and warnings went to all the strategic commands. To Montenegro as well and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You sometimes use the term para-police, and I believe at other times the term paramilitaries was used. Can you tell us what you mean by each of these terms? When you use the term para-police what do you mean, and when you use the term paramilitary, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, what I mean is that a group of people get together, they organise themselves, they get police uniforms, and they introduce themselves as members of the police, and they commit crimes and they loot outside the system of the existing system in the police structure. It's a group, renegades if I can put it that way. They get uniforms, they use the name of police, and they do what they do, commit crimes, loot, rape and so on. As for paramilitaries, we said that paramilitary formations did not exist in the army of Yugoslavia except in the territory of Kosovo where it was the KLA that was the main paramilitary force. It was outside any kind of system. It was armed. It fought and committed crimes against their own people and against the JNA. They are a real paramilitary formation. Within the army of Yugoslavia, there could not have been any such formations, because through orders and warnings and instructions issued by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff it was regulated how volunteers should be taken in. They could not have been grouped, and they had gone through this procedure that had already been explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, I'm not sure if I understand your last answer. Are you saying that the term "paramilitary," as far as you use it, applies exclusively to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We did not have any other renegade groups. All the others, the military conscripts were within the organised legal army that was based on the constitution and law, whereas these were outside that system. They wore uniforms, and they carried weapons, and they were not internationally recognised either as an armed force, and they were not regulated by law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note could Mr. Stamp please switch off his microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were there not groups of persons wearing uniforms committing crimes in Kosovo that were attached to the MUP of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I tried to explain a few moments ago, and then it was said -- or, rather, we ultimately came to it that they were organically part of the MUP or of state security. According to our first information, we thought that they were not, that they were some kind of para-formations wearing police uniforms, and that is why we -- when we found out informed the MUP about that. The reaction to that was the one that I already described on the part of the MUP. At the moment when we found out about them, we sent information about that. They existed before, and it was defined later that they were a reserve force of the MUP and state security, and then we got that explanation. We gave up. They exist, end of story. Such units did not exist --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- As a whole within the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was asking you generally about these units. Do you know of any order from the Supreme Command -- sorry, from the chief of the command, Supreme Command Staff, that paramilitaries were to be disarmed? Or I think maybe we should have a look at --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you look at P1902, please. Very well. I understand that there might be some difficulties with that document. I'll move on quickly. In an area where -- in Kosovo in particular, in Kosovo where the VJ was undertaking combat tasks and there might be civilians in the neighbourhood, was it incumbent on the VJ commanders in those areas to disarm and, if necessary, arrest armed paramilitary formations or members of armed paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff ordered that by way of one of his orders that in the zones the army and all units should check their respective areas, and if they find any paramilitary formations, that is to say such organisations or groups of people armed, in uniform, those who do not belong to their organic structure, they should disarm them, arrest them, and initiate the appropriate procedure. This kind of order does exist and it pertains to these possible paramilitaries. And also there was a deadline involved in terms of when there should be reporting back, and I think you should have a document about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was an interruption in the tone, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of responsibility, well, now we're talking about the 3rd Army there was no such thing this. The commander of the battalion checks his own zone, and then the brigade, and so on; and they did not come across people who wore the uniform of the army of Yugoslavia without belonging to any organised unit according to establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How about other armed formations in the zone of operations of a military unit? Was the responsibility of the command of that unit to disarm these formations in their zone of operations when combat activity was to be undertaken?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. That was regulated precisely through that order, that they search their own area and that they should control their zone of responsibility, that they are responsible for, to check that there were no such groups outside their own units. That was the core of that order. And I think that there was feedback information that in the zones of responsibility of their units there were no armed paramilitary organisations except for these KLA units, and they could not disarm them. They allowed for this possibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- But you know what it's like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, we've had evidence before the Court of many crimes being committed against Kosovo Albanians by armed paramilitary or members of armed paramilitary formations in the presence of VJ units and during operations that VJ units were conducting. Did the security sector receive information about these crimes?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: All the information that was received was processed further, all the information that was received: Commands, security organs, the judiciary. As for these crimes that were committed, they were prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were asked to give an example of -- of persons prosecuted for crimes against international humanitarian law or war crimes, and you mentioned one case of an officer who went along with a group of soldiers was involved in the killing of approximately 10 civilians, some of whom were thrown in a well. Can you recall whether or not the name of that officer was Stojisic, Colonel Stojisic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware, General, that the case in respect to Colonel Stojisic was dismissed?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: General Stojisic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's Colonel Stojisic.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know. At the moment when -- at the moment when a certain case goes before the judiciary, we have no further jurisdiction over these cases unless the prosecutor's office and the investigation organs of the courts do not ask us for additional investigations and additional information regarding such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But General --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The outcome of all of these cases is in the court archives, and the court can give specific answers to this question -- or, rather, the military judiciary can give concrete answer. I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, you referred to that case as --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- As a drastic case. Are you saying that you would not recall the outcome of a case --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: One of the drastic cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you saying that you would not recall the outcome of a case in which a colonel of the VJ is alleged to have killed 10 people, 10 civilians?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I cannot. I really cannot go into that. There are entire lists as to what was done in accordance with General Ojdanic's orders, and you have all these cases listed specifically and their outcomes. It's a long list, and you will probably have an opportunity to hear about this when the court organs testify, because we were not in a position to see how the courts finished their job. We were out there to prevent crimes and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- And to deal with any if committed. You will get specific information without any speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm asking is this: Do you know how many officers of the VJ or how many cases against officers of the VJ were presented by the security organs to the military courts for crimes committed against Kosovar Albanian citizens in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: The security service compiled that within their commands because these crimes happen out in the field in units, so that is how they participate in that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you were --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: As for this number of crimes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the rest of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were the head of the security services or security administration for the army so you can answer whether you know or not how many officers of the VJ were prosecuted or how many cases were presented against officers by the security administration of the VJ in 1999.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: We did not keep such records. Such records were kept by the court and the prosecutor's office. I'm saying again that we did not follow the outcome of these trials unless they gave us additional tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Farkas, that's not the question you're being asked. How many cases did your administration present to the military prosecution authorities which involved officers of the VJ allegedly committing crimes against Kosovo Albanians? Now surely you have records of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my administration did not because this was happening out in the field.
