I already explained that these criminal reports were filed in the units where this actually happened. My administration did not have such crimes committed within it. It is the commands and the security organs of the units concerned that provided this information. It is the courts that had the numbers and everything that happened. The security administration is an institution. It doesn't even have any soldiers. It has drivers and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was an interruption again, interpreters note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So all of this was happening down there in the units and they were in charge of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But, General, according to you General Ojdanic issued orders where these types of crimes were dealt with as a matter of priority. The security organs in the field, in the brigade, in the battalions reported up to your administration. You're saying that you do not know how many cases they prepared against VJ officers in 1999, and that question you can answer yes or no, that you know or you do not know.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's a simple question but it went up the chain of command and that's where the problem was. The security organs integrated into brigade commands and then through the commander's signature this went up the chain of command, this security aspect too, that is to say involving these crimes. We've already explained that there was this bottleneck and that there were these problems and that that did not come up to the chief of General Staff. You have to understand that there is no direct communication between the chief, between me, and the organ down there in the brigade and the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you about a report that crimes were being committed now. I'm asking you about a report upwards that people, VJ members, were being prosecuted. You're saying that you did not get those reports upwards even after the orders of General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying. I didn't put it that way. Again there were problems regarding this reporting up until that moment. After that, things started developing normally again, but just before the war was over new problems cropped up in relation to these units and so on, and the military conscripts who were in Kosovo with their families and now the army was supposed to withdraw and the families were supposed to stay behind and so on and so forth. There were other problems that came to the fore then and then certain crimes were committed and they prevented us from intensively working on clearing this up. From the 17th of May onwards, up until some date --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, General --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- You probably have it in the court reports up until what time this was being cleared up, processed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, you're not answering my question?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- And punishment meted out and I cannot talk about --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. General, I'll move on. Time is very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, how long will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think maybe I could perhaps stop now because there might be re-examination, and he has indicated that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask the interpreters first of all how much slack we have for this evening?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes. Would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's certainly very generous. If the lights go out, we'll -- I don't see any howls or hear any howls of protest from any other quarter. Your re-examination will be how long, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing in re-examination for the time being, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you do it in 10 minutes, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have had evidence -- and I'm moving on to something else. We've had evidence that civilians in Kosovo were armed by the VJ in 1998. Indeed we have evidence that General Samardzic said at --

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm coming to the question, sir. General Samardzic said that 47.000 weapons had been issued in Kosovo to civilians in 1998, to Serb civilians. Did the Ministry of Defence play a role in the issuing of these weapons?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: At that time that you're talking about, I was the assistant minister for civilian defence, and I don't know anything about the distribution of the weapons. I know about the number that was on the basis of my order and the establishment that had been signed was distributed to the civilian structures of the society, the civilian protection unit, the encryption protection unit, the civilian defence, and a little over 6.500 weapons were issued, although the establishment envisaged that there should be about 9.000 people. But we didn't have enough personnel to fill all those posts. This was not just handed out to people. It was placed in depots, and according to my order the weapons were to be distributed in accordance with the achieved degree of mobilisation. As a unit was mobilised weapons were issues. This is all I know about this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. During the conflict, after the 24th of March, there is evidence indicating that what were described in orders as armed non-Siptar population were deployed for operations in conjunction with VJ forces or in support of operations by VJ forces. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the army couldn't distribute, at least not on the basis of the existing establishment. They may have called up the reserve force and then distributed weapons to them, but it is possible that the weapons that you're talking about were distributed to some Civil Protection Units that had been mobilised - I don't know the number now - or the civilian defence units, but in accordance with the establishment constitution and the law --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters doesn't hear the rest of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, I moved on from the distribution of weapons. What I'm asking is this: When armed civilians are deployed for action in support of the VJ as we have had evidence that there were in 1999, during the conflict, do they not come under the jurisdiction of the VJ if any of their members commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, according to this logic they should. The moment they get into the ranks, the moment they line up, if there are not enough uniforms they bear insignia indicating that as of that moment on they belong to an army unit and that they should act or conduct themselves as the army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, you've answered the question. Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where armed civilians are deployed for operations in support of the VJ and individual members of those armed civilians commit crimes during those operations, was it not the responsibility of the organs of the security sector to arrest them?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: Well, the role of the security organs is to arrest anyone who is found in the commission of the crime, and these civilians were part of organised units of the army even if they didn't wear uniforms, and they absolutely were subject to the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: -- Sanctions as the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When -- and I'm moving on to something else now, General, quickly. When you were -- you were reassigned from the ministry of -- of defence to the staff of the Supreme Command, or to become the head of the security administration, wouldn't you agree with me that you were being placed in a position that gave you more responsibility for decision-making at a tactical and strategic level of the VJ than you were before when you were in the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: No. This function in terms of its size and structure is lower than the one that I held before. I was the assistant defence minister covering a whole large sector, the whole system. I was in charge of producing the defence plan for the country, and here I was responsible only for a part of that system, only for the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I had a series of questions in respect of this but I'll just ask you one. We have had evidence that on many occasions bodies were transported from various places in Kosovo to Batajnica and other places in Serbia during the conflict, what is numbering to over 800. When did it first come to your attention as head of the VJ security administration that upwards of 800 bodies of Kosovo Albanians were transferred to Serbia during the time when you occupied that post?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I wasn't aware of the number, but that's something that I heard after the war. I heard after the war that something had happened there and that this was within the purview of the MUP and that some investigations were being carried out, but the military had nothing to do with this. It had no jurisdiction, no tasks to do, and it had no problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Batajnica where most of the bodies were found is a VJ compound on which the MUP had a range. You're saying that you did not receive any information, or you did not know about bodies being buried on this VJ compound?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Protest from Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, if you allow me to say again the question which Mr. Stamp asked the witness, it is not VJ compound. We never heard before that this compound is VJ compound. So the base -- the base for this question I don't know really where my learned friend found. We never heard in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think the evidence was that -- I think the evidence was that this is a VJ compound on which the MUP had a firing range. You had to pass your VJ check-point then a MUP check-point to get there. In any case, the witness has said that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My -- my recollection's similar to Mr. Stamp's, but I wouldn't be prepared to buy on it solidly, so we shall allow you to ask the question without reference to the layout, Mr. Stamp. If you want the witness to clarify whether he has heard nothing about this, then obviously you would be able to make submissions if in fact the basis that you've originally stated is shown to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So, Witness, when you heard -- or I choose to ask you this: Did you not know -- or did you know, did you know, that the area at Batajnica where these bodies were found was part of a VJ compound?

utterances.speaker: GEZA FARKAS
utterances.text: That was not part of a VJ facility. It was quite clearly delineated. There was a high fence. There were two gates, entrance gates. So there were two separate facilities, one next to the other. The military had no jurisdiction over the facility that was used by the MUP. As you said, there were two check-points where you could get into one or the other facility. One was under the jurisdiction of the military and the other was under the jurisdiction of the MUP. The only thing they had in common was the fact that they were next to each other. They were adjacent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes I thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want more time then you have to ask for us to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am finished. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Farkas, that completes your evidence. You will not be required to return tomorrow. You are free to leave as soon as we adjourn, and the link will now be disconnected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber would like to express its gratitude to the audiovisual staff, the interpreters, transcribers, security officers, court staff, for all your cooperation this evening in assisting us to complete the evidence of this -- of this witness. Another day, Mr. Ackerman, perhaps. We will be sitting unusual hours tomorrow to sit around about the Plenary meeting of Judges at noon. We hope to be able to adhere to the schedule announced, which means we will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.27 p.m.,
